summaries.example: Imagine that you see several points showing where Mars appeared in the sky. The points are facts. Kepler used the idea of an oval-shaped path, called an ellipse, to bring those facts together. Whewell said this is how scientific thinking can discover a useful law: the mind adds an organizing idea to observations.
summaries.summary: William Whewell was a wide-ranging nineteenth-century thinker who worked on science, history, education, and morality. He helped make the word “scientist” familiar and gave Faraday the terms “anode,” “cathode,” and “ion.” In philosophy of science, Whewell argued that learning about the world requires two things: what we sense and ideas supplied by the mind. Ideas such as space, time, and cause help us arrange our experiences. He called the mind’s work of joining facts under a useful concept colligation. For example, Kepler used the idea of an ellipse to understand observations of Mars. Whewell believed scientific theories should be tested by their predictions, by whether they explain different kinds of facts, and by whether they become more connected without extra fixes. He also said that science, its history, and the actual work of scientists should inform one another. In morality, he held that conscience is reason applied to moral questions, not merely a feeling. He also connected necessary truths and moral understanding with his religious view that the world and human minds share an underlying order.
key_ideas: Whewell thought knowledge needs both observations and ideas from the mind.
Science is not just counting examples. Scientists organize facts with concepts and then form wider laws.
A strong theory can predict new facts and explain different kinds of events with one idea.
Whewell studied both the history of science and the work of scientists to understand scientific methods.
He thought careful reasoning helps people discover moral rules as well as scientific rules.
summaries.why_it_matters: Whewell’s ideas show that science is an active search for patterns, not a simple pile of observations. They also show why history and real scientific practice can help us think about what science is. His work raises a lasting question: how do facts, ideas, evidence, and reasoning work together? His views about morality show another way philosophers have tried to explain how people can reason about right and wrong.

important_terms.definition: A way of reasoning that uses several observations to reach a broader rule or law.
Bringing many facts together under one helpful idea or pattern.
An idea supplied by the mind that helps organize what we observe, such as space, time, or cause.
Evidence that supports a scientific explanation.
A moral guide that Whewell understood as reason thinking carefully about right and wrong.

questions_to_think_about: Why might observations need ideas before they become useful knowledge?
Is a theory stronger when it predicts something no one has seen yet?
Can one explanation successfully connect very different kinds of events?
How should we use reason when people disagree about what is right?

summaries.example: Consider Newton’s account of gravity. Different investigations concern falling bodies, the Moon, planets, and Jupiter’s satellites. Whewell’s idea of consilience says the theory gains unusual support when one inverse-square gravitational principle unifies these otherwise different domains. The theory does not merely fit facts used to construct it; it reaches beyond them and organizes new classes of phenomena without ad hoc additions.
summaries.summary:
William Whewell developed a historically informed philosophy of science that combines empirical observation with active conceptual construction. He rejected both a purely rationalist picture, in which knowledge comes from reason alone, and an ultra-empiricist picture, in which the mind passively receives sensations. His “fundamental antithesis” distinguishes the ideal contribution of Ideas from the objective contribution of Perceptions. Fundamental Ideas such as Space, Time, Cause, and Substance organize experience; each science may also depend on more particular organizing ideas. Because observation already involves these structures, it is idea-laden rather than theoretically neutral.

Whewell called his method “discoverers’ induction.” Induction begins with facts but adds a conceptual element. Through colligation, a scientist unites facts by superimposing a conception that reveals a common property or cause. Kepler’s use of the ellipse to organize observations of Mars illustrates this process. The scientist may consider several possibilities, but choosing the appropriate conception is not mere arbitrary guesswork. Once a conception has been applied, its shared property can be generalized over cases not yet observed.

A proposed theory must then receive confirmation. Prediction tests whether it correctly covers future or previously unknown cases. Consilience occurs when a theory formed around one class of facts also explains another, different class; Newtonian gravitation is Whewell’s central example. Coherence is the growing unity of a theory as it extends to new phenomena without special, implausible modifications. key_ideas: Whewell’s “fundamental antithesis” holds that knowledge has both an ideal or conceptual side and an objective, perceptual side; neither pure rationalism nor mere sensation is sufficient.
Observation is idea-laden: scientists use conceptual structures, often unconsciously, in determining what facts mean.
Discoverers’ induction is not simple enumeration and not arbitrary guessing. It involves developing, selecting, and applying concepts, then generalizing to unobserved cases.
Prediction, consilience, and coherence support a theory. New predictions are especially valuable, while consilience unifies distinct event kinds under a shared cause.
Whewell argued that the history and practice of science provide material from which a philosophy of science should be tested and developed.

He claimed that empirical inquiry can contribute to recognizing necessary truths once scientific ideas have been sufficiently clarified, and he extended a related developmental account to moral principles.
summaries.why_it_matters: Whewell offers a sophisticated alternative to the picture that science either mechanically collects facts or invents hypotheses without rational guidance. His account emphasizes the creative but disciplined role of concepts, the importance of unexpected evidence, and the value of unifying explanations. It also connects philosophy of science to scientific history and practice: a methodology should be capable of being illustrated by what scientists have actually done. His discussion of necessary truth raises a difficult question about how empirical discovery can lead to claims presented as knowable independently of experience. important_terms.definition: Whewell’s broad account of scientific reasoning: facts are joined by concepts, then a shared property is generalized over observed and unobserved cases.
The mental operation of uniting empirical facts by applying a conception that makes them expressible as a general law.
A mind-provided organizing idea, such as Space, Time, Cause, or Substance, used in forming knowledge.
The clarification of a partly implicit idea so that it can be applied precisely to empirical facts.
A particularly powerful confirmation that one theory successfully unifies different classes of phenomena.
The increasing fit and unity of a theory as it explains additional phenomena without ad hoc changes.
A truth knowable independently of particular experience because it follows necessarily from clearly understood ideas or conceptions.
Whewell’s view that conscience is reason operating on moral subjects, through reflection on basic moral principles.

questions_to_think_about: Does a successful prediction provide stronger evidence than an explanation of facts already known? Why might Whewell think so?
Can a theory’s ability to unify different phenomena support the view that it describes real causes, rather than merely organizing observations?
If observation is always shaped by concepts, how can scientists criticize or replace those concepts?
What is the difference between generating several possible ideas and selecting one through evidence and inference?
Does treating moral principles as rationally discoverable make moral disagreement easier or harder to resolve?

summaries.example: Suppose a student notices that a plant near a window grows toward the light. One observation is not enough for a law. The student records many plants, forms an idea about light and growth, and then checks whether the idea predicts what happens in new cases. If the same idea also helps explain different plants, the evidence is stronger. This resembles Whewell’s view that science joins observations with concepts and tests the resulting theory.
summaries.summary:
William Whewell was a nineteenth-century British scholar who wrote about many subjects, especially the history and philosophy of science and moral philosophy. He also helped scientists with language: he created the word “scientist” and supplied terms later used by Faraday. Whewell’s central idea is that knowledge needs both experience and thought. We receive sensations from the world, but the mind actively organizes them through ideas such as space, time, cause, and substance. This means observation is not completely passive.

Whewell called his approach to scientific discovery “discoverers’ induction.” He thought induction was more than listing examples and expecting a rule to appear. Scientists bring facts together with a conception, or organizing idea. He called this process colligation. Kepler, for example, used the idea of an ellipse to connect observations of Mars’s positions and describe its orbit. The scientist must clarify possible conceptions and use several kinds of inference to decide which one best fits the facts. This is not the same as choosing a theory by an unsupported guess.

After a theory is developed, it must be confirmed. Whewell emphasized prediction, especially successful predictions of facts not yet known. He also emphasized consilience: a theory is especially impressive when it explains a different class of phenomena from the one that first suggested it. Coherence means that a theory becomes more unified as it expands, rather than needing awkward additions. Whewell used Newton’s theory of gravity as an example of these ideas. He also argued that the study of scientific history and actual scientific work should help shape philosophy of science.

Whewell believed that some truths can become necessary once the relevant ideas are clearly understood
key_ideas: Whewell believed knowledge combines what we observe with ideas that the mind contributes.
He disagreed with the view that induction is only a tally of repeated examples.
Scientists use concepts to discover patterns, including patterns involving things they cannot directly observe.
A theory gains support by making successful predictions, explaining new kinds of facts, and fitting together coherently.
The history of science helps us understand how scientific methods actually work.
Whewell thought moral judgment involves reason and reflection, not just a mysterious feeling.
summaries.why_it_matters: Whewell helps us see why scientific thinking requires both evidence and imagination. Facts matter, but facts alone do not automatically arrange themselves into laws. Concepts help scientists find patterns, and predictions and unifying explanations help test whether those patterns are reliable. His approach also encourages us to study what scientists really do instead of discussing scientific method only in the abstract. His moral philosophy adds a related lesson: he believed reason can guide reflection about right and wrong, even though people may disagree or be influenced by their desires.

important_terms.definition: Reasoning from particular observations toward a general rule, though Whewell says it involves more than simply counting examples.
Using a concept to connect separate observations so they can be stated as a general law.
A basic organizing idea, such as space, time, cause, or substance, that the mind brings to experience.
Support for a theory, especially when it successfully predicts facts or explains different kinds of cases.
When one explanation works for different groups of facts and brings them together under a wider law.
A theory becoming more unified as it explains new cases without adding special fixes.

questions_to_think_about: Why might two people looking at the same facts notice different patterns?
What makes a prediction more impressive than simply explaining facts already known?
Why is it useful for one theory to explain several different kinds of events?
Can studying past scientific discoveries reveal rules for doing science?
How could careful reasoning help settle a disagreement about a moral rule?
